prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: システム連携用語表 (language ja).
Grid: 3 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "用語" · longest unbreakable word 16px · one-line width 210px
  col 2: header "英語" · longest unbreakable word 103px · one-line width 163px
  col 3: header "説明" · longest unbreakable word 31px · one-line width 860px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 720px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"A Japanese-language glossary for systems integration: each row pairs a Japanese term with its English equivalent and a short explanatory definition, so readers can identify a concept and then understand it.","reading":"Readers scan the first column for the Japanese term, glance across to the English label for recognition, then read the description for meaning. The first two columns act as a paired index; the third is explanatory prose.","groups":["Columns 1 and 2 belong together as the term/English label pair identifying the same concept.","Column 3 stands apart as the explanatory text and can absorb most wrapping."],"keep_intact":["Japanese technical terms in column 1 where possible, especially compound terms that are hard to reparse after wrapping.","English single-word identifiers in column 2; the longest unbreakable token needs about 103px of text width.","Header labels and the row-identifying first-column values."],"may_wrap":["Description text in column 3, which is long prose and can naturally occupy multiple lines.","Multiword English phrases such as “service level agreement” at spaces.","Longer Japanese terms in column 1 if that column is deliberately narrowed."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[210,160,349],"idea":"Balanced reference layout: keep the Japanese term and English label on one line and give the remaining width to the description."},{"name":"B","widths":[250,125,344],"idea":"Row-header-first layout: maximize the Japanese term column, compress English to just fit its longest single word, and let English phrases wrap."},{"name":"C","widths":[175,145,399],"idea":"Description-first layout: accept wrapping in longer Japanese terms to give the explanatory prose the widest, most readable column."}]}
